meta.tagline: Art nouveau, comic-strip walls and Europe's untidy but lovable capital

pills: Beautiful at second glance, not first

overview.title: Welcome to Brussels
overview.intro: Brussels doesn't try to charm you at first sight: art nouveau mansions stand beside glass EU towers, and the clatter of a flea market is two streets from the elegant arcades. But your breath catches the first time you step into the Grand Place, you come face to face with a Tintin mural on a wall, and in a frietkot queue you hear three languages at once. This city isn't polished, it's layered — it gets more beautiful the more you peel. Take your time; Brussels wins you over on day two.

local_word.definition: Brussels' own brand of humour: self-mocking, gently irreverent towards authority, sweetly sarcastic. Making a statue of a peeing boy your national symbol — that is Zwanze.

rules.title: Stay flexible in a bilingual city
rules.description: Brussels is officially bilingual: street signs come in French and Dutch, and one square can have two names. French dominates, but English works everywhere; start with 'bonjour' and the rest follows.

rules.title: The beauty is up high and in the courtyards
rules.description: Brussels' façades can look tired, but the carvings above doorways, the art nouveau balconies and the inner courtyards will surprise you. Walk without looking up and peeking through gates, and you miss half the city.

rules.title: Give Sunday morning to the flea market
rules.description: The Jeu de Balle flea market has been set up every morning for 150 years; Sunday is its fullest day. Go early, haggle, then have breakfast in the Marolles cafés — this is Brussels' most local morning.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: Train to centre ~20 min · beware Charleroi

quick_facts.label: Getting around
quick_facts.sub: Tap in with a contactless card

tip.label: The Brussels philosophy
tip.text: Don't compare Brussels to Paris; it isn't even entering that race. This city promises an odd corner instead of a perfect square, a good beer table instead of a grand boulevard — set your expectations that way and they'll be exceeded.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: The centre is walkable, the hills are tiring, the metro-tram network is a friend: combine them and forget the idea of a car.

items.title: Airport to the centre
items.description: The train from Zaventem reaches Central in 20 minutes. Read the small print on any ticket that says 'Brussels South Charleroi': that airport is an hour from the city and needs a bus transfer.

items.title: The metro and tram network
items.description: The STIB/MIVB network wraps the city; tap your contactless bank card at the gate and the daily fare cap is calculated automatically. Look at the art in the metro stations — some are small galleries.

items.title: The centre on foot — but hilly
items.description: Most places are walkable from the Grand Place, but the city is hillier than it looks — the Sablon and the Palace sit on the ridge. Use the shortcuts like the lift by the Congress column down to the Lower Town.

items.title: Day-trip trains
items.description: Belgian rail is a day-tripper's paradise: Bruges and Ghent in an hour, Antwerp in 45 minutes. Weekend tickets are discounted; make Brussels your base and sweep Flanders.

items.title: Villo! and the bike lanes
items.description: The shared bikes are cheap, but with the hills and cobbles, cycling Brussels is for the experienced: the canalside and the parks are lovely, the centre's traffic takes courage.

callout.label: Metro tip
callout.text: The metro art tour is free: a giant Tintin wall at Stockel, surrealist works at Porte de Hal. You've already bought the ticket — hop off at a few stations, look around, catch the next train.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: Brussels is a different city in every quarter: the medieval centre, elegant Sablon, bohemian Saint-Gilles, the bureaucrats' European Quarter.

local_word.definition: An old-style neighbourhood tavern: wooden tables, hundreds of beers, yellowed photographs on the wall. In Brussels, the quality of a neighbourhood is measured by the quality of the estaminet on its corner.

items.name: Grand Place and the Ilot Sacré
items.description: Waking up two streets from the world's most beautiful square: museums, arcades and the smell of waffles at your door. Lively at night, touristy on the surface — the practical classic for a first visit.

items.name: Sablon
items.description: The hilltop of antique dealers, master chocolatiers and galleries: a weekend antiques market, and the city's smartest cafés around it. Walking distance to the Royal Museums; prices match the elegance.

items.name: Saint-Gilles
items.description: The district of art nouveau façades, market squares and young coffee roasters: the Horta Museum is here. Few tourists, real neighbourhood life; ten minutes to the centre by tram.

items.name: Sainte-Catherine and Dansaert
items.description: The old fish market square and the Flemish designers' street: the city's best restaurants and bars cluster here. Five minutes to the centre, long dinners guaranteed.

items.name: The European Quarter (Quartier Européen)
items.description: The EU institutions' district: suit traffic on weekdays, calm and discounted hotels at weekends. Next to Cinquantenaire park; sensible if your business is with the EU or you're a weekend bargain hunter.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Brussels' calendar is full of surprises: a flower carpet, a medieval pageant, a light festival — whatever the sky decides.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Greenhouse Season
items.subtitle: Spring · Royal greenhouses, park picnics
items.description: The parks turn green, the terraces go up, and the year's most special rendezvous arrives: the Royal Greenhouses of Laeken open to the public for just a few weeks. The weather is capricious, but the city is at its freshest.

callout.label: April–May tip
callout.text: The Laeken greenhouses open ~3 weeks a year (late April–May): a camellia forest inside palaces of iron and glass. Check the dates ahead and book — this is Brussels' least missable appointment.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Festivals on the Square
items.subtitle: Summer · The Ommegang pageant, the Flower Carpet, open air
items.description: In July the Grand Place travels back in time with the Ommegang medieval pageant; in mid-August (in even years) the square is covered by a giant carpet of begonias. The city has the calm of holiday season, and festivals come one after another.

callout.label: August tip
callout.text: The Flower Carpet runs four days in mid-August in even years: buy the Town Hall balcony ticket to see the carpet from above, and stay for the evening light-and-music show.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Museum and Beer Season
items.subtitle: Autumn · Museum nights, beer weekend
items.description: In September the beer festival fills the Grand Place with wooden casks and the museums begin their evening events; the leaves paint the Cinquantenaire gold. The crowds thin, and the estaminets grow warm.

callout.label: September tip
callout.text: On Heritage Days (September) normally closed art nouveau mansions and EU buildings open their doors for free: the year's only chance to step inside the houses of Horta's students.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Light and Punsch
items.subtitle: Winter · Winter Wonders, the light show, mulled wine
items.description: In December Winter Wonders takes over the city: the Christmas market on the fish market square, a giant Ferris wheel by the canal, a sound-and-light show on the Grand Place. January and February are museum-and-estaminet season: drizzle outside, a quadrupel inside.

callout.label: December tip
callout.text: The Grand Place light show is free, every evening on the hour: the crowds pile into the first showing, so pick one after 9 pm and catch the square half empty.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: The Brussels table is generous: mussel pots, double-fried frites, chocolate in century-old arcades and the deepest beer menu in the world.

local_word.definition: Lambic beer fermented with sour cherries: the best-loved member of Brussels' own family of lightly sour beers. Lambic is made only with the wild yeast in this valley's air — it literally cannot be brewed anywhere else.

items.name: Moules-frites — the national pot
items.description: A pot of mussels with white wine and celery, frites on the side: Belgium's national dish. In season from September to April; using an empty shell as tongs is the proper technique.

items.name: The frietkot ritual
items.description: A cone of double-fried frites with andalouse sauce on top: in Brussels the frietkots work late into the night and every neighbourhood has its favourite. If the queue is long, you're in the right place.
items.tag: In a cone · from the stand with the queue

items.name: The gaufre — plain school
items.description: The Brussels waffle is light and rectangular, the Liège dense and caramelised. Tourist shops sell them under mountains of strawberries and chocolate; locals eat theirs hot and plain, icing sugar at most.
items.tag: Hot and plain · no to the fruit mountain

items.name: A praline arcade crawl
items.description: In the covered Galeries Royales lives the haute couture of chocolate: you're in the city where the praline was invented. Have your box picked piece by piece, and don't forget the sea-salt caramel.
items.tag: In the Galeries Royales · pick the box yourself

items.name: Stoemp and carbonnade
items.description: Stoemp: mashed potato with vegetables, topped with sausage or a fried egg — Brussels home cooking. Carbonnade flamande is beef braised in beer. Eat both in an estaminet, at a wooden table.

items.name: A lambic and gueuze tasting
items.description: Spontaneously fermented lambic, blended champagne-style, becomes gueuze: sour, alive, unforgettable. The historic Cantillon brewery by the canal still works with 1900s methods — the tour includes a tasting.
items.tag: At Cantillon · be open to sour

callout.label: The beer rule
callout.text: Don't panic if the beer menu is as thick as a book: tell the waiter sweet, sour or dark, and they'll solve the rest. Every beer arrives in its own glass — photographing the glass isn't rude, it's tradition.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees the Grand Place; these six open up Brussels' layers.

items.rarity: The house where art nouveau was born
items.name: The Horta Museum
items.description: Victor Horta's own house in Saint-Gilles: the staircase is a spiral of light, every door handle a design lesson. In the home of the man who invented art nouveau, you see the movement at its purest. Tickets are limited — book ahead.

items.name: The Jeu de Balle Flea Market
items.description: The market set up every morning in the heart of the Marolles: old records, dog-eared Tintins, silver forks, strange keepsakes. Haggling included, breakfast in the surrounding cafés — Brussels' most honest morning.

items.rarity: The ninth art on the walls
items.name: The Comic Book Route
items.description: More than sixty giant murals hide on the city's walls, from Tintin to Lucky Luke: take the map and hunt street by street. Start with the Tintin wall in the centre and collect your way towards the Marolles.

items.name: The MIM rooftop
items.description: The rooftop café of the Musical Instruments Museum, in the art nouveau Old England building, looks out over the Lower Town: domes, rooftops, the Atomium in the distance. The museum itself is a surprise too — you tour it listening to the instruments through headphones.

items.rarity: A winter garden of iron and glass
items.name: The Royal Greenhouses of Laeken
items.description: King Leopold II's art nouveau glass palaces: camellias, palms, domed winter gardens. Open only a few weeks a year (April–May) — if your visit coincides, cancel every plan and come here.

items.rarity: On top of the triumphal arch
items.name: The Cinquantenaire arch
items.description: You reach the terrace of the park's colossal triumphal arch through the army museum: all of Brussels at your feet, from the EU towers to the old town. The park is for picnics, the museums are the rain plan.

callout.label: Surrealism tip
callout.text: Book the Magritte Museum for the afternoon: the morning crowds belong to school groups. On the way out, watch the sunset from the Mont des Arts garden two steps away — clouds in bowler hats are not guaranteed, but they happen.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Brussels' traps are concentrated in two streets; know them, and the rest of the city is honest.

items.name: The insistent waiters of Rue des Bouchers
items.description: The iced seafood displays and arm-pulling waiters of the restaurant street are the classic trap: lukewarm mussels, a swollen bill, and the 'free' starter invoiced at the end.
items.instead: Take a parallel street or walk to Place Sainte-Catherine: the same mussel pot, half the price, local customers.

items.name: A strawberry mountain on top, a stale waffle below
items.description: The neon shopfronts around Manneken Pis bury the waffle under fruit, cream and sugar: the sweetest way to hide stale batter.
items.instead: Order it hot and plain: if the batter is fresh, it needs nothing. A Liège waffle straight off a street cart's iron beats most shops.

items.name: 'Belgian chocolate' outlets
items.description: The 'factory price' signs along the tourist drag sell industrial chocolate in gift boxes at triple the price.
items.instead: Climb to the Sablon: in the masters' shops the pralines are picked piece by piece; the price difference is smaller than you think, the difference on the tongue is huge.

items.name: Going to the Atomium with the wrong expectations
items.description: The Atomium is mesmerising from outside; inside it's a long queue plus a modest exhibition, and the disappointment comes bundled with the ticket.
items.instead: Settle for photos from outside and smile at Mini-Europe next door; if you do go in, go for the evening lights, not the exhibits.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Brussels, avoid anywhere that tries to pull you in from the doorway: a good estaminet has locals sitting inside, not a waiter standing outside.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: One layer of Brussels, from the square to the flea market

steps.title: The Grand Place, empty
steps.description: See the gilded guild houses in morning light; drink your coffee at the edge of the deserted square. Stop by Manneken Pis, smile at his size, move on.

steps.title: Mont des Arts + Magritte
steps.description: The city view from the garden terrace, then a dose of surrealism at the Magritte Museum: 'This is not a pipe' — but this is definitely Brussels.

steps.title: Lunch at Sainte-Catherine
steps.description: A mussel pot on the old fish market square (if in season) or a seafood bar counter; alternative: a frietkot cone on a bench on the square.

steps.title: The Sablon and down into the Marolles
steps.description: Fill a box at the master chocolatiers on the Sablon and scan the antique shop windows; then descend into the Marolles and rummage the bric-a-brac shops around the Jeu de Balle.

steps.title: The MIM rooftop or the arch terrace
steps.description: A sunset coffee at the rooftop café of the Old England building; if you have energy left, climb the Cinquantenaire arch and gather the city from above.

steps.title: An estaminet to close
steps.description: Carbonnade or stoemp at a wooden-tabled tavern, with a Trappist in its own glass; make the second beer a gueuze — you drink to Brussels.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Peel the capital layer by layer

steps.title: The classic centre
steps.description: The one-day flow above: Grand Place, Magritte, Sainte-Catherine, Sablon, Marolles, estaminet.

steps.title: Art nouveau and Europe
steps.description: The Horta Museum and a Saint-Gilles façade walk in the morning; Cinquantenaire park and the arch terrace in the afternoon, with the Parlamentarium for the EU side; evening in the Dansaert bars — Flemish design plus cocktails.

steps.title: Comics and lambic
steps.description: The Comics Art Museum and a mural hunt in the morning; the Cantillon lambic tour and tasting in the afternoon; a farewell dinner around the Jeu de Balle — and if it's Sunday morning, the flea market first.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Brussels is bilingual; these five French phrases open every door, and a 'dank u wel' earns you a Flemish smile as a bonus.

items.meaning: Good day — the mandatory first word of every exchange; skip it and you start cold
Thank you — keep 'dank u wel' in reserve for the Flemish side
Please — in Belgium the waiter also says it when setting down your plate
Cheers! — no glass is raised without eye contact
'A gueuze, please' — this sentence promotes you from tourist to guest

checklist.title: Brussels Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Santé! You've lived Brussels layer by layer!
